Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles
WAWR-feeld KOWN-ter-fit MIR-uh-kuhlz
proper noun
Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield (1851–1921), Princeton theologian; Counterfeit Miracles (1918), his lectures defending cessationism.

📖 Biblical Definition

Benjamin B. Warfield was the great Princeton defender of biblical inerrancy and the clearest modern statement of the cessationist position, set down in his 1918 lectures Counterfeit Miracles. Warfield argued from Scripture and from church history that the miraculous gifts—prophecy, tongues, healings, the working of wonders—were the credentials of the apostles and of those on whom the apostles laid hands, given to authenticate the founding revelation of the New Covenant. The signs of an apostle marked the apostle; when the apostolic age closed and the canon was complete, the sign-gifts that accompanied and confirmed inspired revelation ceased with it. He traced the claimed miracles of later centuries—medieval relics and shrine-cures, Roman canonization wonders, Irvingite tongues, and the faith-healing movements of his own day—and found them counterfeit: not the genuine apostolic gift but credulity, imposture, or the ordinary providence of God misread. Warfield did not deny that God answers prayer or heals according to His will; he denied that the office of miracle-worker and the gift of inspired prophecy continue. The dictionary holds Warfield’s cessationism as the Reformed default: God has spoken finally in His Son, the canon is closed, and the church lives by the sufficient written Word, not by fresh revelations.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

B. B. Warfield’s 1918 lectures defending cessationism—the miraculous sign-gifts authenticated the apostolic foundation and ceased with the close of the canon.

COUNTERFEIT MIRACLES, B. B. Warfield’s 1918 lectures on the cessation of the sign-gifts.

Argued the miraculous gifts authenticated the apostles and the founding revelation.

The signs of an apostle ceased when the apostolic age and the canon closed.

Examined medieval, Roman, Irvingite, and faith-healing wonders and found them counterfeit.

Holds the Reformed cessationist default: the sufficient written Word, not fresh revelation.

📖 Key Scripture

2Co 12:12 — "Truly the signs of an apostle were wrought among you in all patience, in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds."

Heb 1:1 — "God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,"

1Co 13:8 — "Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away."

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The charismatic and continuationist movements answer Warfield by claiming the apostolic sign-gifts for the present church; the dictionary holds the cessationist line.

expand to see more

The corruption Warfield exposed is the perennial claim that fresh miracles, new prophecy, and revelatory tongues continue—a claim pressed in his day by the faith-healers and revived in the twentieth-century Pentecostal and charismatic movements, the New Apostolic Reformation, and the prophecy conferences of the present hour. The danger is twofold: it sets a private revelation alongside the closed canon, eroding the sufficiency of Scripture, and it loads tender consciences with false promises of guaranteed healing. Warfield’s historical survey showed how readily credulity, suggestion, and outright fraud counterfeit the genuine work of God.

The principle to recover is the finality of revelation in Christ and the sufficiency of the written Word. God who spoke in many parts and many ways by the prophets has spoken last and fully in His Son; the faith was once delivered to the saints. The sign-gifts authenticated that founding deposit and, their purpose served, ceased. The church does not wait on new oracles; she contends for the faith already given.
